newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Kohl defends Germany's gold revaluing plans.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl defends Germany's gold revaluing plans.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Monday defended his controversial plan to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves, saying the project was "entirely legitimate" and would not harm the central bank's autonomy.

Adressing top bankers at a conference in Switzerland, Kohl said he wanted reasonable talks with the German central bank on the plan that last week triggered an unprecedented rift between the fiercely independent Bundesbank and politicians.
"Let me state here, clearly and categorically: in no way does the revaluation of the Bundesbank reserves amount to an infringement of the independence of the Bundesbank," Kohl said.
"We know from decades of positive German experience that an independent central bank is a prime asset," he added.

The Bundesbank last week issued a strongly-worded statement protesting against Bonn's calls for a transfer of book profits notched up as a result of the revaluation of assets to state coffers this year and next, saying this damaged its independence and undermined Germany's image as a by-the-rules player on EMU.

Bonn's plans, which have triggered massive criticism and calls for Finance Minister Theo Waigel to resign, are to use the proceeds of the revaluation of gold and currency reserves to retire old debt, thus helping it make the grade to take part in Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) from January 1, 1999.

"Germany will do everything to meet both the Maastricht criteria and timetable," Kohl said, predicting a turnaround this year in Germany's stubbornly high unemployment levels, the main barrier to its meeting tough Maastricht debt and deficit goals.

The German central bank is not in principle opposed to revaluing its gold reserves but insists that the process should not take place until 1999, or at least not before the decision as to who will participate in monetary union, in May 1998.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at 13.7 billion marks ($8 billion) versus a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.
The Maastricht Treaty calls on countries to keep their budget deficits at or below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and debt levels at or below 60 percent of GDP.
Kohl, trying to downplay Bonn's rift with the guardians of the deutsche mark, said the timing of the revaluation was the only issue on which the Bundesbank differed with the government.
"Contrary to many reports, the other funds released from reserve assets as a result of a revaluation will on no account be used to plug any gaps in the budget," he said.

"Rather they will be used to reduce the future burden of debt and interest payments, from which in the end the taxpayer stands to benefit, since a total of 20 billion marks will be set aside to redeem the historic burdens of the German Democratic Republic," he said of the debt incurred as a result of the 1990 reunification of West and East Germany.
The developing eastern states would have received some 1,000 billion marks from public budgets by the end of 1997, Kohl said.
"It is therefore entirely legitimate to take the sensible course of moderately revaluing our reserves already at this stage and not to wait for 1999," Kohl said.
Kohl said the revaluation procedure would not distort liquidity conditions so as to trigger an inflation upsurge.

"Contrary to what some people allege, there is...no justification for any loose talk about inflationary dangers," Kohl said, arguing that the Bundesbank would be able to offset gradually any liquidity effects that might result.

While he avoided explicit references to French chances of taking part in EMU folowing the surprise Socialist victory in weekend parliamentary elections, Kohl also said he could "hardly imagine" monetary union without Germany and other large EU countries.

Kohl was speaking at the International Monetary Conference in Interlaken, a three-day annual event attented by more than 100 leading commercial bankers and central bank chiefs. ($ = 1.713 German Marks)
